messages.content: When does the start of turn event occur relative to effects that last until the start of turn?

Per CR 4.2.2, the start phase begins by first ending all effects that last until the 'start of turn,' and then the 'start of turn' event occurs and effects that trigger at the start of turn are triggered. So effects with that duration expire before the start-of-turn triggers fire.
When does the beginning of the action phase event occur?

Per CR 4.3.1, the action phase begins by triggering the 'beginning of the action phase' event. This is distinct from the 'start of turn' event (CR 4.2.2), which occurs earlier during the Start Phase. Auras like Seismic Surge and Embodiment of Earth trigger on the beginning of the action phase, not at the start of turn.
Can players gain priority during the Start Phase?

No. Per CR 4.2.1, players do not get priority during the Start Phase. Triggered-layers created during the start of turn event resolve as if all players are passing priority in succession (CR 1.10.2), meaning the process is automatic without players making interactive decisions.
In what order does the end-of-turn procedure happen?

Per CR 4.4.3, the end-of-turn procedure occurs in this order: (a) reset ally life totals, (b) the turn-player may put a card from hand face-down into an empty arsenal zone, (c) all cards in pitch zones go to the bottom of their decks, (d) the turn-player untaps all permanents they control, (e) all players lose all action and resource points, and (f) the turn-player draws up to intellect. After each step, any triggered effects are added to the stack and resolved before continuing.
When are pitch zones cleared? Can I keep cards in my pitch zone between turns?

No. Per CR 4.4.3c, during the end-of-turn procedure, each player puts all cards in their pitch zone (if any) on the bottom of their deck in any order. This happens as step three of the end-of-turn procedure, so pitch zones are always cleared before the turn ends.
When do 'until end of turn' continuous effects expire?

Per CR 4.4.4, effects that last until the 'until end of turn' or 'this turn' end at the very end of the turn — after the full end-of-turn procedure (CR 4.4.3) has been completed. This is the third and final step of the End Phase.
When do 'until end of next turn' effects expire?

Per CR 4.2.2, effects that last until the 'start of turn' end at the beginning of the Start Phase, before the 'start of turn' event fires. An 'until end of next turn' effect lasts through the opponent's turn and expires at the start of the controlling player's next turn (the 'start of turn' timing), which is when CR 4.2.2 clears those effects.
Can I play action cards during an opponent's turn?

Generally no. Per CR 8.1.1b, an action card can only be played/activated when the stack is empty, and per CR 8.1.1d, if an action card is played as though it were an instant, it can be played any time the player has priority but does not cost an action point. Action cards with the ability to be played as instants are the only way to play them outside of your own action phase.
At the very start of my turn, I have an 'end of next turn' effect active. When exactly does it expire?

Per CR 4.2.2, during the Start Phase, effects that last until the 'start of turn' end first, before the 'start of turn' event is triggered. An 'until end of next turn' effect generated on an opponent's turn would expire at the beginning of your Start Phase — before your start-of-turn triggers fire.
When does a player draw cards at end of turn? What if they already have more cards than their intellect?

Per CR 4.4.3f, the turn-player draws cards until the number in their hand equals their hero's intellect. If it is the first turn of the game, all other players also draw up to intellect. If a player already has at least that many cards in hand, they draw no cards. This step occurs after untapping (4.4.3d) and losing action/resource points (4.4.3e).
Can I put a card from hand into my arsenal if it's already occupied at end of turn?

No. Per CR 4.4.3b, the turn-player may put a card from their hand face-down into an empty arsenal zone they own. The zone must be empty, so if the arsenal zone already contains a card the player cannot place another one there.
Do triggering effects during the end-of-turn procedure resolve all at once, or step by step?

Per CR 4.4.3, after each individual step in the end-of-turn procedure, if a triggered effect has triggered, those triggered-layers are added to the stack and then the stack resolves fully before the next step begins. This means triggered effects are handled between each sub-step, not all at the end.
Does the turn-player get priority during the End Phase?

No. Per CR 4.4.1, players do not get priority during the End Phase. The 'beginning of the end phase' event occurs and any triggered-layers resolve automatically (CR 4.4.2), and the end-of-turn procedure (CR 4.4.3) likewise resolves without interactive priority windows.
What triggers at the beginning of the end phase versus at the end of the turn?

Per CR 4.4.2, the 'beginning of the end phase' event occurs first during the End Phase and effects that trigger at this point fire and resolve. Then, after the full end-of-turn procedure (CR 4.4.3) completes, the turn ends (CR 4.4.4), where 'until end of turn' effects expire. Cards like Bloodrot Pox and Ponder tokens trigger at the beginning of the end phase, not at the end of the turn.
What happens to action points and resource points at end of turn?
Per CR 4.4.3e, all players lose all action points and resource points as the fifth step of the end-of-turn procedure. This applies to all players, not just the turn-player.
Does the turn-player start their action phase with 1 action point or 0?

Per CR 4.3.2, the turn-player receives 1 action point as the second step of the action phase beginning. Per CR 4.3.2a, effects that trigger when a player gains an action point do not trigger from gaining this action point, and per CR 4.3.2b, replacement effects that modify gaining an action point also do not apply to this initial grant.
When does the action phase end?

Per CR 4.3.4, the action phase ends when the stack is empty, the combat chain is closed, and both players pass priority in succession. All three conditions must be met simultaneously for the game to proceed to the End Phase.
If an effect gives a player an extra turn, when does that turn happen?

Per CR 4.0.3c, an extra turn granted by an effect is taken immediately after the specified turn. So if an effect says 'you take an extra turn after this one,' that extra turn begins as soon as the current turn ends, before any other player takes their turn.
Do ally life totals reset during cleanup or at some other time?

Per CR 4.4.3a, as the first step of the end-of-turn procedure, all allies' life totals are reset to their base life, modified by any counters on the object. This happens before arsenal, pitch, untap, or draw steps.
During the start-of-game procedure, if an effect triggers that only fires 'during a player's turn,' does it trigger?

No. Per CR 4.1.8b, if an effect would only trigger during a player's turn, it does not trigger during the start-of-game procedure. The rules cite Victor's triggered effect as an example — a gold token created during start-of-game would not trigger Victor because it is not during a player's turn.
When exactly does a chain link resolve versus when does the combat chain close?

Per CR 7.6.2, a chain link resolves at the beginning of the Resolution Step — it becomes a resolved chain link and go-again action points are granted. The combat chain does not close at this point; the attacker may play another attack (CR 7.6.3a). The combat chain only closes when, after the stack is empty, all players pass in the Resolution Step without a new attack being played (CR 7.7.2a), at which point the Close Step begins (CR 7.7).
In what order do the steps of a chain link resolve?

Per CR 7.0.1, a chain link resolves in seven steps in order: Layer Step, Attack Step, Defend Step, Reaction Step, Damage Step, Resolution Step, and (if the chain closes) the Close Step. Each step has its own priority windows and actions allowed.
When does a 'hit' trigger fire? Is it during the Damage Step or later?

Per CR 7.5.5, an attack is considered to have hit if it deals damage to an attack-target during the Damage Step. The hit-event is identical to a deal physical damage event and occurs during the Damage Step (CR 7.5.2a). Triggered effects that fire 'when this hits' are triggered during the Damage Step when the hit-event occurs, and then added to the stack for resolution afterward.
Can a defense reaction be played during the Defend Step?

No. Per CR 7.4.1 and CR 7.4.2b, defense reactions can only be played during the Reaction Step by a player that controls a hero as an attack-target. The Defend Step (CR 7.3) is for declaring non-defense-reaction defending cards from hand and public equipment.
Can an attack reaction be played during the Defend Step?

No. Per CR 7.4.2a, attack reactions can only be played by the player that controls the attack during the Reaction Step of combat (CR 7.4). Neither player plays reactions during the Defend Step; that step is reserved for declaring defending cards (CR 7.3.2).
What happens to attacks and reactions on the stack when the combat chain closes?

Per CR 7.7.3, when the combat chain closes, the 'combat chain closes' event occurs, and all attacks and reactions currently on the stack are put into their owner's graveyard. They do not resolve — they are simply discarded to the graveyard.
Can I play another attack during the Resolution Step?

Yes. Per CR 7.6.3a, the turn-player may play or activate another attack during the Resolution Step, including attack action cards or weapon/ability attacks. If an attack is added to the stack during the Resolution Step, the Resolution Step ends and the Layer Step begins for the new chain link (CR 7.6.3).
If my attack has go again, when exactly do I gain the action point?

Per CR 8.3.5b, if go again is an ability of an attack on the active chain link, the controlling player gains 1 action point at the beginning of the Resolution Step of combat (CR 7.6.2). This is distinct from go again on a non-attack layer (CR 8.3.5a), where the action point is gained after all other resolution abilities resolve.
Can the combat chain be open while there are no active attacks?

Yes, briefly. Per CR 7.6.1, the Resolution Step is a game state where the active chain link has just resolved — the chain link becomes resolved but the combat chain is still open. The attacker has priority to add a new attack. Only after all players pass in succession with an empty stack does the combat chain close (CR 7.7.2a).
When are equipment returned to their equipped zones after combat?

Per CR 7.7.5, during the Close Step, when the stack is empty, all permanents remaining on the combat chain return to their respective zones — equipment and weapons return to their respective equipped zones. Any other permanent returns to the permanent zone (i.e., the arena).
If the active-attack ceases to exist before the Damage Step, what happens?

Per CR 7.7.2c, if the active-attack of the active chain link ceases to exist before damage is calculated, the Close Step begins as a game state action. The combat chain closes immediately without a Damage Step or Resolution Step.
If an attack has no legal targets at the beginning of the Attack Step, what happens?

Per CR 7.2.2, at the beginning of the Attack Step, at least one of the attack's attack-targets must still be a legal target. If none are legal, the Attack Step ends and the Close Step begins immediately (CR 7.7.2b). Note that only one target needs to be legal at this point — if additional targets become illegal later, combat continues (CR 7.2.2a).
Can I defend with the same equipment on two different chain links in the same combat chain?

Yes, as long as the equipment returns to its equipped zone between chain links. Per CR 7.7.5, permanents on the combat chain return to their zones during the Close Step. However, within a single chain link, per CR 7.0.5b, a card cannot be added as a defending card if it is already a defending card on that chain link.
Can a player defend with more than one card from hand against an attack without dominate?

Yes. Per CR 7.3.2a, if the attack-target is a hero, their controller may declare any number of non-defense-reaction cards from their hand and/or public equipment permanents they control as defending cards. The only restriction on multiple hand cards is dominate (CR 8.3.4), which limits defending to one card from hand.
During the Reaction Step, who gets priority first — the attacker or the defender?

Per CR 7.4.2, the turn-player gains priority first during the Reaction Step. In a standard two-player game, the attacking player is the turn-player and gains priority first. The defending player may play defense reactions only when they have priority (CR 7.4.2b).
If two or more players declare defending cards for the same attack-target, who goes first?

Per CR 7.3.2e, if two or more players may declare defending cards for an attack-target, they do so in clockwise order starting with the player that controls the attack-target. So the defending hero's controller always declares their cards first.
Does declaring defending cards cost an action point or go through the stack?

No. Per CR 7.3.2, declaring cards as defending cards during the Defend Step is not considered playing those cards — it does not incur any play cost, does not add them as a layer on the stack, and does not resolve any resolution abilities on those cards. It is a free declaration.
What is a triggered layer and how does it differ from a card layer?

Per CR 1.6.2c, a triggered-layer is a layer created by a triggered effect. Unlike a card-layer (CR 1.6.2a), which is a card moved to the stack when played, a triggered-layer is created in response to an event or game state condition meeting a trigger condition (CR 6.6.5). Triggered-layers are added to the stack before the next player receives priority (CR 6.6.6) and resolve like any other layer in LIFO order.
When can a triggered ability trigger? Does the trigger effect need to exist before the triggering event?

Yes. Per CR 6.6.5a, a triggered effect must exist before an event or change in state occurs that satisfies its trigger condition for it to be triggered. If a triggered effect is generated after the triggering event occurs, it does not retroactively trigger. The only exception is inline-triggered effects (CR 6.6.2), which trigger as they are generated if the condition is immediately met.
If two triggered effects trigger simultaneously, who orders them onto the stack?

Per CR 6.6.6b, if two or more triggered-layers would be created simultaneously, the turn-player selects a player, then each player in clockwise order adds all their pending triggered-layers to the stack in an order they choose, starting with the selected player. Each player controls the order of their own triggers; the turn-player only determines who goes first.
What is the difference between an optional and a mandatory triggered ability?

Per CR 6.6.1 and CR 1.8.3, mandatory triggered effects use language like 'when' or 'whenever' without 'may,' and they must trigger and create a triggered-layer when their condition is met. Optional triggered effects include the word 'may' in their abilities text. Per CR 6.6.5e, if a triggered effect has a trigger limit and that limit is reached, even mandatory triggers will not create a triggered-layer.
What is an activated ability and how is it different from a resolution ability?

Per CR 5.2.1, an activated ability is an ability that can be activated to put an activated-layer on the stack. It is always written in the format '[LIMIT?] [TYPE] -- [COST]: [ABILITIES] [CONDITION?].' A resolution ability (CR 1.7.3b) generates effects only when a layer with that ability resolves on the stack. Activated abilities require a player to actively trigger them and pay a cost, whereas resolution abilities fire automatically when their layer resolves.
If the source of a triggered-layer ceases to exist before the triggered-layer resolves, does the triggered-layer still resolve?

Yes. Per CR 1.7.1a, activated-layers and triggered-layers exist independently of their source. If the source of an activated-layer or triggered-layer ceases to exist, it does not prevent the resolution of that layer. The layer remains on the stack and resolves normally.
When does a static ability become functional?

Per CR 1.7.4, a static ability is functional when its source is public and in the arena. There are several exceptions: play-static abilities are functional when the source is public in any zone (CR 1.7.4e), property-static abilities are functional at all times (CR 1.7.4f), and while-static abilities are functional when their while-condition is met (CR 1.7.4g). Meta-static abilities function outside the game (CR 1.7.4d).
Can I activate an activated ability of a card in my hand?

Only if the ability's cost can only be paid when the source is private or the activation condition specifies the source is in a private zone. Per CR 5.2.4, if an activated ability meets this condition, it is functional when the source meets that requirement. Examples include abilities with 'Discard this:' as the cost (e.g., Vigorous Windup), which can be activated from hand (CR 5.2.4a).
What is a state-based triggered effect and how does it trigger?

Per CR 6.6.1c, a state-based triggered effect triggers based on a game state rather than an event. Per CR 6.6.5c, it triggers if the game state did not initially meet the trigger condition, then changes to meet it. If a state-based triggered effect is generated while the game state already meets the condition, it also triggers immediately.
If a triggered-layer has a state-trigger condition and the game state no longer meets it when the layer resolves, what happens?

Per CR 5.3.2b, if the layer is a triggered-layer created by a triggered effect with a state-trigger condition, that condition must be met by the current game state when the layer resolves — otherwise the layer fails to resolve. The Phantasm example in CR 5.3.2b illustrates this: if the defending card's power drops below 6 before the Phantasm triggered-layer resolves, it fails to resolve.
Can two or more replacement effects apply to the same event?

Yes. Per CR 6.4.4, a replacement effect can replace an event that has been modified by another replacement effect, as long as the effect is active for that modified event. Per CR 6.5.1, if two or more replacement effects could replace the same event, they are applied based on an order determined by the turn-player and then each controlling player. The order of types applied is: self/identity-replacement, then standard-replacement, then prevention (CR 6.5.3-6.5.5).
What is the difference between a fixed-prevention effect and a shielding-prevention effect?

Per CR 6.4.10i, a fixed-prevention effect prevents a specific amount of damage from one triggering event only — any remaining prevention amount is not used for subsequent events. Per CR 6.4.10j, a shielding-prevention effect acts as a shield that persists across multiple events until its total prevention amount is exhausted. Shielding effects are typically phrased as 'prevent the next X damage,' while fixed effects are typically phrased as 'prevent X of that damage.'
Can a prevention effect be applied to damage that 'cannot be prevented'?

Yes, but with limited effect. Per CR 6.4.10h, if an effect states a prevention effect cannot prevent the damage of an event, the prevention effect still applies to the event but its prevention amount is not reduced. However, any additional modifications to the event by the prevention effect (such as destroying the source) still occur. This means Enchanting Melody still gets destroyed even if the damage cannot be prevented.
Can Arcane Barrier be used after arcane damage has already been dealt?

No. Per CR 8.3.8, Arcane Barrier is a static ability that means 'If you would be dealt arcane damage, you may pay N{r} to prevent N of that damage.' It is a replacement effect that must be applied before the damage event occurs (CR 6.4.3). Once arcane damage has been dealt, it is too late to apply Arcane Barrier.
Is Arcane Barrier mandatory or optional?

Arcane Barrier is optional. Per CR 8.3.8, the ability uses the word 'may,' meaning the player chooses whether or not to pay N{r} to prevent N damage. This makes it an optional prevention effect per CR 1.8.3.
Does Arcane Barrier prevent physical damage?

No. Per CR 8.3.8, Arcane Barrier specifically reads 'if you would be dealt arcane damage,' meaning it only applies to arcane damage. Per CR 6.4.10c and CR 8.5.3f, a prevention effect that specifies a damage type cannot prevent another type of damage, so Arcane Barrier provides no protection against physical ({p}) damage.
What is Ward and what type of damage does it prevent?

Per CR 8.3.20, Ward N means 'If you would be dealt damage, destroy this to prevent N of that damage.' Ward does not specify a damage type, so per CR 6.4.10c, the prevention applies to any and all damage types — physical, arcane, or generic. Ward prevents all damage types by default.
Is Ward optional or mandatory?

Ward is mandatory when triggered — the card is destroyed and the damage is prevented automatically. Per CR 8.3.20, the wording 'destroy this to prevent N of that damage' is not written with 'may,' making it a mandatory prevention effect. The player does not choose whether to apply Ward; it activates whenever the source would be dealt damage (of any type).
What is Spellvoid and from which zone must the source be to use it?

Per CR 8.3.15, Spellvoid N means 'If you would be dealt arcane damage, you may destroy this to prevent N of that damage.' Spellvoid requires the source to be able to be destroyed, meaning the object with Spellvoid must be a permanent in the arena (CR 8.3.15a). If the controlling player cannot destroy the object, they cannot apply the optional prevention effect.
Is Spellvoid optional?

Yes. Per CR 8.3.15, Spellvoid uses the word 'may,' making it an optional prevention effect (CR 1.8.3). The player chooses whether or not to destroy the Spellvoid source to prevent the arcane damage. If they cannot destroy it, the option is unavailable per CR 8.3.15a.
Does Spellvoid prevent physical damage?

No. Per CR 8.3.15, Spellvoid specifically states 'if you would be dealt arcane damage,' so it only prevents arcane damage. Per CR 6.4.10c, a prevention effect specifying a damage type cannot prevent a different type, so Spellvoid provides no protection against physical or generic damage.
What is Amp and when is the bonus applied?

Per CR 8.5.47, Amp is a continuous effect that means 'the next time an event the player controls would deal arcane damage this turn, instead it deals that much arcane damage plus N.' The Amp bonus applies to the next arcane damage event controlled by that player during the current turn. It is consumed upon the first arcane damage event it applies to.
Does Amp apply to all arcane damage this turn or just the next instance?

Just the next instance. Per CR 8.5.47, Amp N means the next time an event the player controls deals arcane damage this turn, it deals that much plus N. After the first qualifying arcane damage event, the Amp effect is consumed and does not apply to subsequent arcane damage events that turn.
Can Amp apply to arcane damage dealt by an opponent's effect?

No. Per CR 8.5.47, Amp specifies 'an event the player controls.' The player who has the Amp effect must control the damage-dealing event for Amp to apply. Damage events controlled by an opponent are not modified by your Amp.
What is Arcane Shelter and how does it differ from Arcane Barrier?

Per CR 8.3.37, Arcane Shelter N means 'If you would be dealt arcane damage, destroy this to prevent N of that damage.' Unlike Arcane Barrier (CR 8.3.8), which requires paying N{r} and is optional, Arcane Shelter automatically destroys itself to prevent damage. Arcane Shelter is mandatory when triggered (no 'may'), and the prevention is a fixed-prevention effect tied to the destruction of the source.
Is there a difference between how physical damage replacement effects and arcane damage replacement effects work?

Per CR 8.5.3b, physical damage is damage dealt by an object using its power value during the Damage Step of combat, and arcane damage is damage dealt by an effect specifically dealing arcane damage. Per CR 8.5.3e, an effect that triggers from a specific type of damage being dealt does not trigger from another type, and per CR 8.5.3f, a prevention or modification effect specific to one type cannot modify another type. The mechanics work the same way, but they are type-gated.
If a prevention effect reduces a damage event to zero, is the attack still considered to have hit?

No. Per CR 7.5.5b, if the hit-event is modified by replacement effects such that no damage is dealt by the active-attack to the attack-target, it is no longer a hit-event and the attack is not considered to have hit. The rules cite Feign Death as an example: if all damage is prevented, the hit does not occur.
What does Go Again mean for a non-attack action card?

Per CR 8.3.5a, if go again is an ability of a non-attack layer on the stack, the controlling player gains 1 action point after all other resolution abilities have resolved (per CR 5.3.5). This allows the player to play another action card that turn, assuming they have available actions.
Can an object have more than one go again ability?

No. Per CR 8.3.5c, an object cannot have more than one 'go again' ability. If an effect would give the 'go again' ability to an object that already has it, that part of the effect fails. This means stacking multiple go again sources on the same object does not grant extra action points.
What does Dominate do and which zone does it restrict defending from?

Per CR 8.3.4, Dominate means 'this can't be defended by more than one card from hand.' Per CR 8.3.4a, if an attack with dominate is already defended by a card from hand, no additional card from a player's hand can be added as a defending card. Per CR 8.3.4b, defense reaction cards from hand also cannot be played while dominate is active and the attack is already defended by a hand card. Dominate only restricts hand cards — equipment and arsenal cards (like Ambush cards) are not restricted.
Does Dominate prevent defending with equipment?

No. Per CR 8.3.4, Dominate specifically restricts cards coming from a player's hand. Equipment cards are permanents in equipped zones, not cards from hand. Per CR 8.3.4a, only cards that 'come from a player's hand' are restricted. Equipment defending is unaffected by Dominate.
If an attack already has two cards from hand defending it and then gains dominate, are the defending cards removed?

No. Per CR 8.3.4c, if an attack is defended by two or more cards from hand and then the attack gains dominate, no cards are retroactively removed from defending. Per CR 1.0.2b, restrictions and requirements do not retroactively change the game state. Dominate only prevents future additions, not existing ones.
What is Phantasm and when does the triggered layer fail to resolve?

Per CR 8.3.13, Phantasm is a triggered-static ability meaning 'Whenever this is defended by a non-Illusionist attack action card with 6 or more {p}, destroy this.' Per CR 8.3.13a, the triggered-layer is put on the stack when the state condition is met. When the triggered-layer resolves, per CR 5.3.2b, if the game state condition is no longer met (e.g., the defending card's power has been reduced below 6), the triggered-layer fails to resolve and does not destroy the attack.
If a Phantasm attack is destroyed before the Damage Step, does the combat chain close?

Yes, in most cases. Per CR 8.3.13b, if an attack is destroyed by Phantasm before damage for its chain link has been calculated, the combat chain closes. However, if the attack is destroyed by Phantasm after damage has been calculated, the combat chain does not close.
Does Phantasm trigger if defended by an Illusionist attack action card with 6 or more power?

No. Per CR 8.3.13, Phantasm specifically reads 'non-Illusionist attack action card with 6 or more {p}.' If the defending card is an Illusionist attack action card (even with 6 or more power), the trigger condition is not met and Phantasm does not trigger.
What is Spectra and what happens when a Spectra object is targeted by an attack?

Per CR 8.3.14, Spectra is both a static ability ('this can be attacked') and a triggered-static ability ('when this becomes the target of an attack, destroy this'). Per CR 8.3.14a, an object with Spectra can be the target of an attack even if it is not a living object. Per CR 8.3.14b, when an object with Spectra becomes the target of an attack, a triggered-layer is put on the stack that, when resolved, destroys the Spectra object.
What is Reprise and when is its condition checked?

Per CR 8.4.3, Reprise is a label for a resolution ability typically written as 'Reprise - If the defending hero has defended with a card from their hand this chain link, [EFFECTS].' Per CR 8.4.3a, the condition is checked on resolution of the attack — it does not retroactively generate effects if the condition is met after resolution.
When is the Crush condition checked — at the time of the hit or later?

Per CR 8.4.2, Crush is a triggered-static ability written as 'When this deals 4 or more damage, [EFFECTS].' The trigger condition fires at the time the damage-dealing event occurs — it is not limited to the Damage Step. Per CR 8.4.2a, the Crush ability is conditional on an event that deals damage, not just a hit-event. This means Crush can trigger from any damage-dealing event of 4 or more damage produced by the source card, not only from a combat hit during the Damage Step.
What is Surge and how does it differ from Crush?

Per CR 8.4.8, Surge is a label for a resolution or static ability typically written as 'Surge - If this deals N damage, [EFFECTS].' Surge is typically a conditional resolution ability that checks if a specific damage threshold is met when the ability resolves, whereas Crush (CR 8.4.2) is a triggered-static ability that fires as a trigger when the damage event of dealing 4 or more damage occurs. Surge is conditional at resolution; Crush is event-triggered.
What is Rupture and when does it activate?

Per CR 8.4.6, Rupture is a label for an ability typically written as 'Rupture - If this is played as chain link 4 or higher, [EFFECTS].' A Rupture effect is a conditional ability that checks whether the card was played as the fourth or later chain link in the current combat chain.
What does Reload do and is it mandatory?

Per CR 8.5.23, Reload is an optional discrete effect meaning 'if the player's arsenal is empty and they choose to do so, move it from the player's hand to their arsenal face-down.' It requires the arsenal to be empty and is fully optional — the player chooses whether to reload. Per CR 8.5.23a, if the player has two or more arsenal zones, all of those zones must be empty for reload to be eligible.
What does Opt N do?

Per CR 8.5.22, Opt is a discrete effect meaning 'the player looks at the top N cards of their deck, then puts any number of those cards on the top or bottom of their deck in any order.' Per CR 8.5.22a, if the deck has fewer than N cards, the player looks at all cards in the deck and puts them back in any order. If the deck is empty, the opt effect fails (CR 8.5.22b).
What does Battleworn do and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.3.2, Battleworn is a triggered-static ability meaning 'When the combat chain closes, if this defended, put a -1{d} counter on it.' The trigger fires when the combat chain closes (during the Close Step, CR 7.7), and is conditional on the card having defended during that combat chain.
What does Temper do and how is it different from Battleworn?

Per CR 8.3.10, Temper is a triggered-static ability meaning 'When the combat chain closes, if this defended, put a -1{d} counter on it, then destroy it if it has zero {d}.' Unlike Battleworn (CR 8.3.2), which only places a counter, Temper additionally destroys the source if placing the counter reduces its defense value to zero.
What does Blade Break do?

Per CR 8.3.3, Blade Break is a triggered-static ability meaning 'When the combat chain closes, if this defended, destroy it.' Unlike Battleworn or Temper, Blade Break always destroys the source if it defended, regardless of any counters or remaining defense value.
What does Boost do and when is a card considered to have 'boosted'?

Per CR 8.3.9, Boost is an optional additional-cost play-static ability meaning 'As an additional cost to play this, you may banish the top card of your deck. If you do, if it's a Mechanologist card, this gets go again.' Per CR 8.3.9a, if a player pays the additional cost (banishing the top card), they are considered to have boosted and the played card is considered boosted — even if the banished card is not a Mechanologist card.
What does Channel do and what happens if the flow counter requirement isn't met?

Per CR 8.4.4, Channel is a label for an ability written as 'Channel [SUPERTYPE] - At the beginning of your end phase, put a flow counter on this then destroy it unless you put a [SUPERTYPE] card from your pitch zone on the bottom of your deck for each flow counter on it.' If the player cannot or does not put the required number of supertyped cards from their pitch zone on the bottom of their deck, the permanent is destroyed.
What does Charge do and what is the difference between charging and putting a card into the soul another way?

Per CR 8.5.29, Charge is a discrete effect meaning 'move a card from the player's hand to their hero's soul.' Per CR 8.5.29b, moving a card to a hero's soul from a rule or effect other than charge is not considered charging. This distinction matters for cards and abilities that trigger specifically on the charge event (e.g., Solflare triggers — CR 8.4.9).
What is Solflare and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.4.9, Solflare is a label for an ability typically written as 'Solflare - When this is charged to your hero's soul, [EFFECTS].' It triggers specifically when the card is charged (moved from hand to soul via the charge effect, CR 8.5.29). Per CR 8.5.29b, placing a card in the soul by any other means does not trigger Solflare.
What does Overpower do and is it different from Dominate?

Per CR 8.3.22, Overpower is a static ability meaning 'This can't be defended by more than one action card.' It restricts action cards of any type from defending, not just cards from hand. By contrast, Dominate (CR 8.3.4) restricts cards specifically from hand. A player could still defend an Overpower attack with two equipment pieces, but could not defend with more than one action card regardless of zone.
What does Intimidate do and is the banished card returned at end of turn?

Per CR 8.5.10, Intimidate is both a discrete effect and a delayed-triggered effect. To intimidate a player, they banish a random card from their hand face-down, and then at the beginning of the end phase, it returns to their hand. Per CR 8.5.10a, the player is considered intimidated even if they had no cards to banish. Per CR 8.5.10c, if there are two separate intimidate effects, each only returns the cards banished by its own effect.
What does Scrap do?

Per CR 8.3.32, Scrap is a play-static ability meaning 'As an additional cost to play this, you may banish an item or equipment from your graveyard.' If the player pays this cost, they are considered to have scrapped. Per CR 8.3.32b, a player cannot scrap if they have no item or equipment in their graveyard to banish.
What does Ambush do and from what zone does it allow defending?

Per CR 8.3.28, Ambush is a while-static ability meaning 'While this is in your arsenal, you may defend with it.' Normally cards in the arsenal cannot be used to defend. Ambush creates an exception allowing the card to be used as a defending card directly from the arsenal zone.
What does Heave do and what does it create?

Per CR 8.3.18, Heave N is a hidden triggered ability meaning 'While this is in your hand, at the beginning of your end phase, you may pay N{r} and put this face-up into your arsenal. If you do, create N Seismic Surge tokens.' The ability is optional (uses 'may') and is a hidden triggered ability (CR 5.4.7b), meaning the player decides whether to reveal and activate it from their private hand.
What does Blood Debt do and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.3.11, Blood Debt is a triggered-static ability meaning 'While this is in your banished zone, at the beginning of your end phase, lose 1{h}.' Per CR 8.3.11a, Blood Debt only triggers if its source is public (face-up) in the banished zone at the beginning of the owner's end phase. If the card is face-down in the banished zone, Blood Debt does not trigger.
What does Guardwell do?

Per CR 8.3.34, Guardwell is a static ability meaning 'When the combat chain closes, if this defended, put -1{d} counters on it equal to its {d}.' Unlike Battleworn which puts one -1{d} counter, Guardwell puts a number of -1{d} counters equal to the card's current defense value, potentially reducing its defense to zero over time.
What does Piercing N do?

Per CR 8.3.23, Piercing is a static ability written as 'Piercing N' which means 'If this is defended by an equipment, it gets +N{p}.' This bonus applies whenever the attack is defended by any equipment, giving the attack bonus power for each point of N the ability specifies.
What does Protect do and who can use it?

Per CR 8.3.31, Protect is a static ability meaning 'You may defend any hero attacked by an opponent with this.' It allows a player to defend with the card for any allied hero, not just their own hero. Per CR 7.3.2e, players with Protect cards declare their defending cards in clockwise order after the defending hero's controller.
What is Quell?

Per CR 8.3.19, Quell N means 'If you would be dealt damage, you may pay N{r} to prevent N of that damage. If you do, destroy this at the beginning of the end phase.' Quell prevents any type of damage (not just arcane) optionally for a resource cost, but also schedules the source's destruction at the beginning of the end phase when used.
What does Ephemeral mean for a card?

Per CR 8.3.21, Ephemeral is both a meta-static ability ('you can't start the game with this in your deck') and a static ability ('if this would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, instead it ceases to exist'). Per CR 8.3.21a, players cannot include Ephemeral cards in their card-pool. Per CR 8.3.21b, a card that ceases to exist from Ephemeral is removed from the game entirely.
When does a Quicken token trigger and what does it do?

Per CR 8.6.1, a Quicken token is an aura with the triggered-static ability 'When you play an attack action card or activate a weapon attack, destroy this then the attack gains go again.' The trigger fires whenever the controller plays an attack action card or activates a weapon attack. It then destroys itself and grants the triggering attack the go again ability.
When does a Runechant token trigger and what does it do?

Per CR 8.6.3, a Runechant token is an aura with the triggered-static ability 'When you play an attack action card or activate a weapon attack, destroy this and deal 1 arcane damage to target opposing hero.' It triggers whenever the controller plays an attack action card or activates a weapon attack, then destroys itself and deals 1 arcane damage to a target opposing hero.
Does a Runechant token trigger on non-attack action cards?

No. Per CR 8.6.3, the Runechant trigger condition is specifically 'When you play an attack action card or activate a weapon attack.' Playing a non-attack action card (such as an instant or action) does not trigger Runechant.
What is a Spectral Shield and what damage type does Ward 1 prevent?

Per CR 8.6.8, a Spectral Shield token is an Illusionist aura with the static ability 'Ward 1.' Per CR 8.3.20, Ward N means 'If you would be dealt damage, destroy this to prevent N of that damage.' Ward does not specify a damage type, so per CR 6.4.10c, it prevents any type of damage — physical, arcane, or generic.
What is a Frostbite token and what does it do?

Per CR 8.6.10, a Frostbite token is an Elemental aura with two abilities: a static ability 'Cards and abilities cost you an additional {r} to play or activate,' and a triggered-static ability 'At the beginning of your end phase or when you play a card or activate an ability, destroy this.' Frostbite increases the cost of all cards and abilities by 1{r} for its controller, and it destroys itself at the beginning of the end phase or whenever its controller plays a card or activates an ability.
What is a Zen State token and what does it do?

Per CR 8.6.5, a Zen State token is a Ninja aura that enters with 1 balance counter and has two abilities: 'At the beginning of your action phase, destroy this unless you remove a balance counter from it,' and 'If you would be dealt damage, prevent 1 damage of that damage.' Zen State provides a passive prevention of 1 damage from any damage event, and it persists as long as a balance counter can be removed each action phase.
Does Zen State's prevention apply to all damage types?

Yes. Per CR 8.6.5, Zen State reads 'If you would be dealt damage, prevent 1 damage of that damage.' Per CR 6.4.10c, since no damage type is specified, the prevention applies to any and all damage types — physical, arcane, or generic. It prevents 1 point from any single damage event.
When does Seismic Surge token activate and what does it do?

Per CR 8.6.2, a Seismic Surge token is an aura with the triggered-static ability 'At the beginning of your action phase, destroy this then the next Guardian attack action card you play this turn costs {r} less to play.' It triggers at the beginning of the action phase (CR 4.3.1), destroys itself, and generates a cost-reduction effect for the next qualifying Guardian attack that turn.
When do Embodiment of Earth and Embodiment of Lightning tokens trigger?

Their trigger windows differ. Per CR 8.6.11, Embodiment of Earth has a triggered-static ability that reads 'At the beginning of your action phase, destroy this' (CR 4.3.1), and a static ability that grants +1{d} to non-attack action cards you control while they are defending. Per CR 8.6.12, Embodiment of Lightning has a single triggered-static ability that reads 'When you play an attack action card, destroy this and the attack gains go again.' Embodiment of Lightning does not have a beginning-of-action-phase trigger — it only destroys itself when an attack action card is played.
When does a Soul Shackle token trigger?

Per CR 8.6.7, a Soul Shackle token is an aura with the triggered-static ability 'At the beginning of your action phase, banish the top card of your deck.' It triggers at the beginning of the action phase (CR 4.3.1) and automatically banishes the top card of the controller's deck. Soul Shackle does not destroy itself — it remains until another effect removes it.
What is an Agility token and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.6.28, an Agility token is an aura with the triggered ability 'At the start of your turn, destroy this, then your next attack this turn gets go again.' It triggers at the start of turn (CR 4.2.2), destroys itself, and the next attack the controller makes that turn gains go again.
What is a Might token and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.6.26, a Might token is an aura with the triggered ability 'At the start of your turn, destroy this, then your next attack this turn gets +1{p}.' It triggers at the start of turn, destroys itself, and the next attack that turn gains +1{p}. Note this is 'start of your turn' (CR 4.2.2), not 'beginning of action phase.'
When does a Ponder token trigger and what does it do?

Per CR 8.6.17, a Ponder token is an aura with the triggered ability 'At the beginning of your end phase, destroy this and draw a card.' It triggers at the beginning of the end phase (CR 4.4.2), destroys itself, and the controller draws a card.
What is Rune Gate and from what zone can cards be played with it?

Per CR 8.3.27, Rune Gate is a play-static ability meaning 'If you control Runechants equal to or greater than this's {r} cost, you may play it from your banished zone without paying its {r} cost.' It allows the card to be played from the banished zone for free, provided the controller has enough Runechant tokens in the arena.
What does Meld do and how does it affect a split-card's cost?

Per CR 8.3.38, Meld is a static ability meaning 'You may pay twice the base cost of this to play both halves of this.' Per CR 8.3.38b, Meld sets the asset-cost before increases and decreases are applied. Per CR 8.3.38c, a melded card has the properties of both of its sides: both names and the combination of all abilities, supertypes, types, and subtypes. Per CR 5.3.4d, when a melded card resolves for the first time, only the right-side resolution abilities generate effects; on the second resolution, only left-side abilities generate effects.
What is Combo and what is required for its condition to be met?

Per CR 8.4.1, Combo is a label for a static ability typically written as 'Combo - If [NAMES] was the last attack this combat chain, [EFFECTS].' The condition checks whether a card with the specified name(s) was the most recent attack on the combat chain before the current one. The condition is evaluated when the Combo ability resolves.
What is Fusion and does a player have to pay it?

Per CR 8.3.17, Fusion is an optional additional-cost play-static ability written as '[SUPERTYPES] Fusion' meaning 'As an additional cost to play this, you may reveal (a/an) [SUPERTYPES] card(s) from your hand.' It is optional — the player chooses whether to pay it. Per CR 8.3.17a, if paid, the player is considered to have fused the specified supertypes and the card is considered fused, which may unlock conditional abilities.
What is a Spellbane Aegis token and what does Spellvoid 1 do on it?

Per CR 8.6.18, a Spellbane Aegis token is an aura with the static ability 'Spellvoid 1.' Per CR 8.3.15, Spellvoid N means 'If you would be dealt arcane damage, you may destroy this to prevent N of that damage.' So Spellbane Aegis lets the controller optionally destroy it to prevent 1 arcane damage.
What is an Aether Ashwing token and what does its Arcane Barrier 1 do?

Per CR 8.6.15, an Aether Ashwing token is a Draconic Illusionist dragon ally with 1{p} and 1{h} and the static ability 'Arcane Barrier 1.' Per CR 8.3.8, Arcane Barrier 1 means 'If you would be dealt arcane damage, you may pay 1{r} to prevent 1 of that damage.' The Aether Ashwing's controller can optionally spend 1 resource to prevent 1 arcane damage.
Can I use the Arcane Barrier on an Aether Ashwing after I've taken damage from the same arcane source?

No. Per CR 8.3.8 and CR 6.4.3, Arcane Barrier is a replacement effect that must be applied before the damage event occurs. Once arcane damage has been dealt and the event has completed, it is too late to apply Arcane Barrier retroactively.
What is a Courage token and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.6.22, a Courage token is an aura with the triggered ability 'When you play an attack action card or activate a weapon attack, destroy this and the attack gets +1{p}.' It triggers when the controller plays an attack action card or activates a weapon attack — the same trigger window as Runechant (CR 8.6.3) and Quicken (CR 8.6.1).
What is an Ash token and what does its Material ability do?

Per CR 8.6.14, an Ash token is a Draconic Illusionist ash with the static ability 'Material - While this is under a permanent, that object has phantasm.' Per CR 8.4.5, Material is a label for an ability that applies while the token is under a permanent. When an Ash token is under a permanent (via the Transform effect or similar), that permanent gains the Phantasm ability (CR 8.3.13).
What is continuous effect staging and why does it matter?

Per CR 6.3.1, continuous effects that modify objects are applied using the staging system, grouped into stages and applied in ascending order. Stage order matters because an effect applied in an earlier stage may change whether a later-stage effect even applies. For example, an effect that modifies types (stage 4) could change whether a power-modifying effect (stage 8) targets the right object. Within a stage, substage order (CR 6.3.3) and timestamp order (CR 6.3.4) further determine the sequence.
If two continuous effects that would give power to an attack are generated at the same time, who decides the order they apply?

Per CR 6.3.4b, if two or more effects start to apply to an object at the same time, the turn-player decides the order those effects apply. This decided order is only used to determine the order of effects with the same timestamps. Once the order is decided, it cannot be changed.
Does a continuous effect that removes a property also remove properties added by other effects?

No. Per CR 6.3.6, continuous effects that remove a property or part of a property from an object do not remove properties or parts of properties that were added by another effect. For example, Erase Face removes base class and talent types, but cannot remove class or talent supertypes gained from effects like Brand with Cinderclaw.
If a layer-continuous effect has a variable value X, when is X determined?

Per CR 6.2.2b, if a layer-continuous effect has variable values such as X, those values are determined when the continuous effect is generated (when the layer resolves) and do not change thereafter. The exception is if the effect applies to an object that does not yet exist, in which case variables are determined when the effect first applies to that object.
What is a self-replacement effect and when is its condition evaluated?

Per CR 6.4.7, a self-replacement effect is a replacement effect that applies to a preceding effect generated by the same ability or a leading connected ability. It is typically written as '[EFFECT]. [CONDITION], instead [MODIFICATION].' Per CR 6.4.7b, the condition of a self-replacement effect is evaluated at the time the preceding effect is generated — not when the card first resolves — meaning if the condition depends on undetermined parameters, it is evaluated when those parameters are determined.
What is a layer-continuous effect versus a static-continuous effect?

Per CR 6.2.2, a layer-continuous effect is generated by the resolution of a layer on the stack and typically has a specified duration. Per CR 6.2.3, a static-continuous effect is generated by a static ability and never has a specified duration — it starts when the static ability becomes functional and ends when that ability becomes non-functional. Layer-continuous effects have fixed durations; static-continuous effects persist as long as their source ability is active.
What is a discrete effect versus a continuous effect?

Per CR 6.1.1, a discrete effect is an effect that changes the game state by producing an event and has no duration — after the event completes, it has no further influence. Per CR 6.2.1, a continuous effect modifies the state and properties of objects or the rules of the game and continues for its specified duration or for as long as its source ability is functional.
If the stack is not empty, can the top layer resolve if it is an attack that is the current active chain link?

No. Per CR 5.3.1, if the stack is not empty and all players pass in succession, the top layer of the stack resolves — except the Layer Step of combat (CR 7.1). During the Layer Step, the attack sits on the stack until all players pass, then the Layer Step ends and the Attack Step begins, at which point the attack resolves per CR 7.2.3.
What zone must a card be in to be played normally?

Per CR 5.1.1a, a player can only play cards from their hand or arsenal zones unless otherwise specified by a rule or effect. Cards in other zones (graveyard, banished zone, deck) cannot normally be played.
How are asset-costs calculated when playing a card?

Per CR 5.1.6a, asset-cost calculation happens in four steps: first, rules define the starting asset-cost; second, effects that set an asset-cost are applied; third, effects that increase an asset-cost are applied; fourth, effects that reduce an asset-cost are applied (but never below zero). If two or more effects apply at the same step, they are applied in timestamp order (CR 6.3.4).
What is the action asset-cost for playing an action card versus playing it as an instant?

Per CR 5.1.6b, the action asset-cost starts at zero. If the card has the type 'action' and is not played as an instant, the action cost starts at one action point instead. Per CR 8.1.1d, if an action card is played as an instant, it does not cost an action point.
At what step is a card considered 'played'?

Per CR 5.1.10, the card is considered played at the ninth and final step of the play process — the 'Play' step — after all asset-costs and effect-costs have been paid. At that point, the player regains priority. Per CR 5.1.2, the card is moved to the stack at the very first step (Announce), but it is not considered played until all costs are paid.
If a card's target is no longer legal when the layer resolves, does it still resolve?

Per CR 5.3.2a, if a layer has a resolution ability with a targeted effect, and at least one target was declared when the layer was put onto the stack, at least one of those targets must still be a legal target when the layer resolves — otherwise the layer fails to resolve. If at least one target remains legal, the layer resolves normally for legal targets.
If a defense reaction cannot become a defending card when it resolves, what happens?

Per CR 5.3.2c and CR 7.4.2d, if a defense reaction card cannot become a defending card on the current chain link when it resolves, the layer fails to resolve. The card is cleared from the stack (typically going to the graveyard) without generating its effects or becoming a defending card. CR 7.4.2d provides the example of dominate preventing a second hand-played defense reaction from resolving.
What is the order of go again in layer resolution?

Per CR 5.3.5, go again is the fourth step of layer resolution — it occurs after all other resolution abilities have generated their effects (step three, CR 5.3.4). This means all the card's other effects resolve before the action point is granted. Per CR 8.3.5a, this applies specifically to non-attack layers; for attacks, go again is granted at the beginning of the Resolution Step (CR 8.3.5b).
Can I play a card as an instant if it's an action card?

Yes, if an effect allows it. Per CR 8.1.1d, if an action card is played as though it were an instant, it is still considered an action, but it can be played any time the player has priority and does not cost an action point. Whether or not a specific action card can be played as an instant depends on whether an effect grants that permission.
What does 'last known information' mean and when is it used?

Per CR 1.2.3, last known information about an object is a snapshot of the state of that object immediately before it ceased to exist. Per CR 1.2.3a, if a rule or effect requires information about a specific object that no longer exists, last known information is used instead. It includes all parameters, history, and effects applicable to that object at the time it still existed (CR 1.2.3b) and is immutable (CR 1.2.3c).
Does a restriction take precedence over an allowance?

Yes. Per CR 1.0.2, a restriction takes precedence over any requirement or allowance, and a requirement takes precedence over any allowance, subject to effects directly superseding rules (CR 1.0.1a). If one effect says you cannot do something and another says you may, the restriction wins.
What is a hidden triggered ability and how does it work?

Per CR 5.4.7b, a hidden triggered ability is both a while-static ability and a triggered-static ability where the while-condition specifies that the source is private or in a private zone. If the triggered condition is met while the ability is functional and the source is private, the owner may decide to trigger the effect. If they do, the source becomes public and a triggered-layer is added to the stack. The source remains public until the triggered-layer resolves or ceases to exist, then returns to being private.
What happens when a triggered-layer is added to the stack — can targets be declared at that point?

Yes. Per CR 6.6.6a, when a triggered-layer is added to the stack, the controlling player must declare the parameters of all abilities of that layer, including modes and all legal targets. If no legal targets can be declared for a targeted effect, the triggered-layer ceases to exist and is not added to the stack.
If an object has a conditional static ability like 'while attacking, this gets +2{p},' when is the condition evaluated?

Per CR 6.2.3d, if a static-continuous effect has a conditional generation, that condition is evaluated at all times. The effect is generated when the condition is met and ceases to exist when the condition is no longer met. So 'while attacking, this gets +2{p}' is continuously checked — the +2{p} applies exactly when and as long as the object is attacking.
Can a player activate an ability of a private source? What happens to the source?

Yes, under specific conditions. Per CR 5.2.4b, if a player activates an ability of a private source, the source of the ability becomes public until either the activated-layer resolves or ceases to exist, or the source ceases to exist. When an object becomes public this way, it does not trigger any abilities and cannot be replaced by any replacement effects.
If I control a Frostbite token, do my defense reaction cards also cost an additional resource to play?

Yes. Per CR 8.6.10, Frostbite's static ability reads 'Cards and abilities cost you an additional {r} to play or activate.' This applies to all cards, including defense reactions, instants, and any other cards the controller plays. Additionally, Frostbite destroys itself 'at the beginning of your end phase or when you play a card or activate an ability,' so it would be destroyed when the defense reaction is played.
If I have a Frostbite token in the arena, does it get destroyed if I activate an equipment ability?

Yes. Per CR 8.6.10, Frostbite's triggered-static ability reads 'At the beginning of your end phase or when you play a card or activate an ability, destroy this.' Activating an equipment ability is activating an ability, so Frostbite would be destroyed when you do so.
Can a Runechant token deal arcane damage to a hero that has Spellvoid active?

Yes, but the Spellvoid player can optionally prevent it. Per CR 8.6.3, when a Runechant triggers, it deals 1 arcane damage to a target opposing hero. Per CR 8.3.15, Spellvoid N means 'If you would be dealt arcane damage, you may destroy this to prevent N of that damage.' The defending player can choose to destroy their Spellvoid source to prevent the 1 arcane damage from the Runechant.
What is an Eloquence token and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.6.23, an Eloquence token is an aura with the triggered ability 'When you play a non-attack action card, destroy this and the card gets go again.' It triggers when the controller plays a non-attack action card — meaning a card with the type Action that does not have the subtype attack (such as an instant or a non-attack action card). Defense reaction cards and attack reaction cards are separate types (CR 1.3.2c) and are not 'action cards,' so playing them does not trigger Eloquence.
If multiple Runechant tokens are in the arena when I play an attack action card, do they all trigger simultaneously?

Yes, all Runechant tokens trigger simultaneously when the trigger condition is met. Per CR 6.6.6b, if two or more triggered-layers would be created at the same time, the turn-player selects a player, then each player in clockwise order adds all their pending triggered-layers to the stack in an order they choose. Each Runechant deals 1 arcane damage to a target opposing hero, so multiple Runechants deal damage to potentially different targets.
What is a Confidence token and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.6.35, a Confidence token is an aura with the triggered ability 'At the start of your turn, destroy this, then the next attack action card you play this turn can't be defended by more than 2 non-block cards.' It triggers at the start of turn (CR 4.2.2), destroys itself, and creates a conditional restriction on how the next attack action card can be defended.
Does Overpower restrict defending with a block card?

No. Per CR 8.3.22, Overpower means 'This can't be defended by more than one action card.' Cards with the type 'Block' are not action cards (CR 1.3.2c lists the deck-card types as Action, Attack Reaction, Block, Defense Reaction, Instant, Mentor, and Resource). Block cards are a separate type and are not restricted by Overpower.
Can I play a card from my graveyard if an effect says I may?

Yes, if an effect explicitly allows it. Per CR 5.1.1a, players can normally only play cards from their hand or arsenal, but this is 'unless otherwise specified by a rule or effect.' If an effect grants the ability to play from the graveyard (such as Rune Gate allowing play from the banished zone, CR 8.3.27), that overrides the default restriction.
What is a Fealty token and how does it sustain itself?

Per CR 8.6.31, a Fealty token is a Draconic aura with two abilities: 'Instant -- Destroy this: The next card you play this turn is Draconic,' and 'At the beginning of your end phase, if you haven't created a Fealty token or played a Draconic card this turn, destroy this.' To sustain Fealty, the controller must either create a new Fealty token or play a Draconic card each turn, otherwise it is destroyed at the beginning of the end phase.
What is a Vigor token and when does it trigger?

Per CR 8.6.27, a Vigor token is an aura with the triggered ability 'At the start of your turn, destroy this, then gain {r}.' It triggers at the start of turn (the 'start of turn' event per CR 4.2.2), destroys itself, and the controller gains 1 resource point.
How does the resolution of a melded split-card work on the stack?

Per CR 5.3.4d, if the layer is melded and it is its first time being resolved, only the right-side resolution abilities generate their effects, then resolution stops and the turn-player gains priority. On its second time being resolved, only the left-side resolution abilities generate their effects, then resolution continues normally. This means a melded card resolves in two separate passes on the stack.
If a triggered effect has a trigger limit of once per turn and an opponent's effect prevents it from triggering once, does that prevent count toward the limit?

Yes. Per CR 6.6.5f, if the triggered effect is triggered but an effect prevents the triggered-layer from being created and added to the stack, the triggering still counts toward the trigger limit. The rules provide Katsu plus Tripwire Trap as the example: the prevented trigger exhausts Katsu's once-per-turn limit.
What does Coronet Peak's activation ability do, and what keyword does it have?

Coronet Peak is an Ice Equipment Head with the Blade Break keyword. Its Action ability costs 3 resources and forces a target hero to discard a card unless they pay 1 resource. Blade Break means that when the combat chain closes after Coronet Peak defends, it is destroyed. The card has 2 defense.
What happens when Coronet Peak defends and the combat chain closes?

Coronet Peak has Blade Break, which triggers when the combat chain closes if this card defended during that combat chain. On resolution, Coronet Peak is destroyed and goes to the graveyard. This applies regardless of whether the attack hit or was blocked — the trigger fires at combat chain close, not at hit.
Can Coronet Peak's Action ability be used while defending, or only on your turn?

Coronet Peak's Action ability uses the 'Action' timing, which means it can only be used during your own action phase on your turn. It cannot be used as an instant-speed response during an opponent's turn or while you are defending. The Blade Break effect, on the other hand, is a triggered ability that fires at combat chain close whenever this card defends.
How does Fyendal's Spring Tunic gain energy counters?

At the start of your turn, if Fyendal's Spring Tunic currently has fewer than 3 energy counters, you may optionally put one energy counter on it. This trigger is optional — you do not have to add the counter. The tunic can hold a maximum of 3 energy counters at any time.
What is the activation effect of Fyendal's Spring Tunic?

Fyendal's Spring Tunic has an Instant activated ability: remove 3 energy counters from it to gain 1 resource. This is usable at instant speed, meaning you can activate it during the combat chain or in response to effects on the stack. It also has Blade Break, so it is destroyed if it defends.
Can you activate Fyendal's Spring Tunic on your opponent's turn?

Yes. Fyendal's Spring Tunic's resource ability has Instant timing, so it can be activated at any time you could play an instant — including during the opponent's turn and during the combat chain. The start-of-turn trigger to add an energy counter, however, only fires at the beginning of your own turn.
What does Arcanite Skullcap do when you have less life than your opponent?

If you have less life than your opponent, Arcanite Skullcap gains +1 defense and Arcane Barrier 3 as a continuous bonus. Arcane Barrier 3 allows you to pay up to 3 resources to prevent that much arcane damage that would be dealt to you — the damage prevented equals the resources spent, up to 3. Arcanite Skullcap also has Battleworn, so each time it defends a combat chain, it receives a -1 defense counter at chain close.
What is the Battleworn keyword and how does it interact with Arcanite Skullcap?

Battleworn is a triggered ability: when the combat chain closes, if this card defended during that chain, put a -1 defense counter on it. For Arcanite Skullcap, this means every time you block with it the skullcap permanently loses 1 defense. Once its defense reaches 0 or below it is still functional but has no blocking value. The card is not automatically destroyed by Battleworn — only the Temper keyword destroys on reaching 0 defense.
What does Heartened Cross Strap do and what does it cost to activate?

Heartened Cross Strap has an Action ability that destroys itself as its cost. When you activate it, the next attack action card you play this turn costs 2 resources less. The ability also has Go again, so you gain an action point when this resolves, allowing you to play another card immediately. The strap has 0 defense and is Generic Equipment.
Can Heartened Cross Strap's ability be used during the opponent's turn?

No. Heartened Cross Strap uses Action timing, not Instant timing. Action-speed abilities can only be used during your own action phase. You cannot activate it to reduce a cost during your opponent's turn or in response to effects on the stack.
How does Ironhide Helm work when you defend with it?

When you defend with Ironhide Helm, you may optionally pay 1 resource. If you do, Ironhide Helm gains +2 defense for that combat chain and also gains the triggered ability 'when the combat chain closes, destroy Ironhide Helm.' This means paying the resource dramatically increases its blocking value but guarantees it will be destroyed at chain close. If you do not pay the resource, Ironhide Helm defends for 0 and survives.
What is the difference between Ironhide Helm, Ironhide Legs, and Ironhide Plate?

All three Ironhide pieces have the same mechanic: when you defend with them you may pay 1 resource to give that piece +2 defense and a 'destroy when the combat chain closes' trigger. The difference is their equipment slot — Ironhide Helm is a Head piece, Ironhide Legs is a Legs piece, and Ironhide Plate is a Chest piece. All three have 0 base defense and are Generic Equipment.
If you pay the resource for Ironhide Plate, can you avoid it being destroyed at chain close?

No. Once you pay the resource, Ironhide Plate gains both the +2 defense and the 'destroy when the combat chain closes' trigger. These are granted together as a package — you cannot get the +2 defense without also accepting the destruction trigger. The destruction fires at the close of the same combat chain.
Can equipment abilities be used as responses on the combat chain?

It depends on the ability's timing. Equipment with Instant-speed abilities (like Fyendal's Spring Tunic's energy ability) can be activated during the combat chain. Equipment with Action-speed abilities (like Heartened Cross Strap or Coronet Peak) can only be activated on your own action phase turn. Equipment that activates as an Attack Reaction (like Blacktek Whisperers) can only be used in response to an attack declaration. Always check the ability keyword — Action, Instant, Attack Reaction, or Defense Reaction — to determine when it can be used.
Can you equip multiple pieces of equipment in the same slot?

No. Each equipment slot (Head, Chest, Arms, Legs) can only hold one piece of equipment at a time. If you equip a new piece to a slot that is already occupied, the existing piece is placed in the graveyard. Most equipment is also Legendary, which means you can only have one copy in your deck.
What is the once-per-turn restriction on equipment activations?

Equipment abilities marked as 'Once per Turn' can only be activated once during each player's turn, not once per round. Equipment like Volzar the Lightning Rod explicitly states 'Once per Turn Instant.' If an equipment does not say 'Once per Turn,' it can typically be activated multiple times per turn, subject to cost and other conditions. The engine tracks exhaustion (tap) as the primary restriction for weapons and some equipment.
When does Big Bully's crowd-boos trigger fire?

Big Bully's trigger fires when it attacks a hero. At that moment, if the controller of Big Bully has more life than the defending hero, the crowd boos the attacker. This is a triggered ability that checks the health comparison at the time Big Bully declares as an attack. If the attacker does not have more life, nothing happens.
What happens to Big Bully's power if you've been booed this turn?

Big Bully has a continuous ability: if you've been booed this turn, this card's base power is doubled. Big Bully has a base power of 4 (red version), so after being booed it has 8 base power. This doubling applies at the time the card attacks, so if you were booed earlier in the turn by any effect, Big Bully benefits immediately when it attacks.
Does Big Bully boo you even if you played it on a turn you already got booed?

Yes, as long as the condition is met (you have more life than the defending hero), Big Bully will trigger the crowd-boos effect again. The 'if you've been booed this turn' doubling checks whether you have been booed at all this turn, so a second boo from Big Bully does not double-double the power — the doubling is a state check, not a stacking multiplier. However, having been booed once is enough for the doubling to apply.
What are Command and Conquer's two separate effects?

Command and Conquer has two effects. First, a continuous effect active while it is on the combat chain: defense reaction cards cannot be played this chain link, preventing the defending hero from responding with cards like Sink Below or Pummel. Second, a triggered on-hit effect: when Command and Conquer hits a hero, all cards in their arsenal are destroyed and go to the graveyard. Command and Conquer costs 2 resources, has 6 power, and is a Generic Action Attack.
Can the defending player play a defense reaction against Command and Conquer?

No. Command and Conquer's text reads 'Defense reaction cards can't be played this chain link,' which is a static restriction active as soon as the card attacks. This prevents the defending hero from playing any defense reaction cards, including Sink Below, Pummel, or other reactions that would normally be legal on the defending step.
When does Command and Conquer's arsenal-destruction effect trigger?

The arsenal-destruction effect is an on-hit trigger: it fires when Command and Conquer hits a hero, meaning after the attack resolves and damage is dealt. If the defending hero blocks Command and Conquer successfully (reduces it to 0 damage or the attack does not hit), the arsenal destruction does not occur. Only a successful hit triggers the effect.
What happens if Command and Conquer hits but the opponent has an empty arsenal?

If the opponent's arsenal is empty when Command and Conquer hits, the on-hit effect does nothing — there are no cards to destroy. The hit still counts and all other effects resolve normally. The arsenal destruction effect only destroys cards that exist in the arsenal at the time of resolution.
What is Chain of Brutality's condition for gaining go again and its on-hit effect?

Chain of Brutality gains go again and its on-hit effect only if it has 6 or more power at the time it attacks. The condition is checked when it attacks. If met, it gains go again (granting an action point on resolution) and the following conditional on-hit effect: when this hits a hero, the next attack action card you play this turn has 6 base power. Chain of Brutality has a base power of 2 (red version) and costs 0.
How can Chain of Brutality reach 6 power to gain its go again?

Chain of Brutality starts at 2 power (red version) and needs to reach 6 or more to unlock its abilities. This requires a +4 or greater power boost from other effects — for example, playing Pummel targeting it (which requires the attack to have cost 2+, and Chain of Brutality costs 0 so this would not apply), or using cards like a power-buffing attack reaction. Common methods include having turn-effects that grant a base-power boost from earlier cards played that turn.
If Chain of Brutality's on-hit effect fires, does the next attack action card played that turn gain exactly 6 power or set its base power to 6?

Chain of Brutality's on-hit effect sets the next attack action card's base power to 6 — it does not add 6 to existing power. This means if that next attack action already has a higher base power, it would actually be lowered to 6. Any additional power modifiers applied after the base-power assignment still apply on top of the 6.
When does Crown of Dominion create a Gold token?

Crown of Dominion creates a Gold token 'when you equip Crown of Dominion,' meaning the trigger fires when the equipment enters the arena — specifically when you put it into your head equipment slot. In the engine this is registered on the 'enters_arena' event. The Gold token is created under your control at that time. Crown of Dominion also makes your hero Royal as a continuous static effect.
Does Crown of Dominion trigger when it replaces a previously equipped head piece?

Yes. The trigger says 'when you equip Crown of Dominion,' which fires any time the card moves into your head equipment slot. If you had a different head piece that was destroyed to make room, Crown of Dominion still creates a Gold token as it enters the arena. The trigger fires on entry regardless of what was there before.
What does Codex of Frailty do when you play it?

When you play Codex of Frailty, each hero (both players) may put an attack action card from their graveyard face-down into their arsenal, provided their arsenal is empty. Each hero that does must then discard a card. After resolving for all heroes, you create a Ponder token under your control and a Frailty token under each opponent's control. Codex of Frailty also has Go again, granting you an action point.
Can a hero use Codex of Frailty's effect if their arsenal is already full?

No. A hero can only participate in the arsenal-filling effect if their arsenal is currently empty. Per the rules, an effect that would put a card into a full arsenal fails. If the arsenal already has a card in it, that hero skips the effect (and therefore does not have to discard either, since the discard is conditional on successfully placing the card).
What token does Codex of Frailty create under your control versus your opponent's?

Codex of Frailty creates a Ponder token under your own control and a Frailty token under each opponent's control. In a two-player game, this means you get Ponder and your opponent gets Frailty. Ponder is a beneficial token for you (draws a card at end of your end phase), while Frailty is a debuff for your opponent (their arsenal attacks and weapon attacks have -1 power until it is destroyed at end phase).
What does the Frailty token do?

Frailty is a Generic Token Aura with a static effect: your attack action cards played from arsenal and weapon attacks have -1 power. This effect applies continuously while Frailty is in your arena. At the beginning of your end phase, Frailty is destroyed. It does not affect attack action cards played from hand — only those played from arsenal or weapon attacks from your equipped weapons.
What is the Ponder token?

Ponder is a Generic Token Aura with a triggered ability: at the beginning of your end phase, destroy Ponder and draw a card. This fires at the start of your end phase, so you draw a card and then Ponder is destroyed. It is created by cards like Codex of Frailty and Codex of Inertia under your control as a reward for playing those cards.
What does Codex of Inertia do when played, and how does it differ from Codex of Frailty?

Codex of Inertia has each hero put the top card of their deck face-down into their arsenal (if their arsenal is empty), then each hero that does discards a card. You create a Ponder token for yourself and an Inertia token for each opponent. The key difference from Codex of Frailty is the source of the arsenal card: Frailty uses an attack action from the graveyard, while Inertia uses the top card of the deck — any card type. Both have Go again.
What does the Inertia token do?

Inertia is a Generic Token Aura. At the beginning of your end phase, Inertia is destroyed, then you put all cards from your hand and arsenal on the bottom of your deck. This is a powerful debuff — it forces you to lose your entire hand and any arsenal card at the start of your end phase when Inertia is destroyed. The effect triggers at the beginning of the end phase.
What does Shifting Tides do at the start of each turn?

Shifting Tides is an Aura that triggers at the start of its controller's turn. It reveals and pitches (sends to graveyard) the top card of your deck. If that pitched card was blue (pitch value 3), Shifting Tides is moved to the bottom of your deck instead of being destroyed. If the revealed card was not blue, Shifting Tides itself is destroyed and goes to the graveyard. If your deck is empty when the trigger fires, Shifting Tides is destroyed.
Is Shifting Tides destroyed if the card it pitches is red or yellow?

Yes. Shifting Tides' survival depends on the top card being blue (pitch value 3). If the top card is red (pitch 1) or yellow (pitch 2), Shifting Tides is destroyed at that start of turn. The card checks pitch value specifically — blue pitch value 3 is the condition for Shifting Tides to survive and go to the bottom of the deck.
What does Steal Victory do when it defends?

Steal Victory is a Reviled Brute Block card with the triggered ability: when this defends, steal an aura token the attacking hero controls.
